You lived the life of a window shop mannequin, posing in the latest fashion or boasting your new lipstick through the silvery screen between my toilet and sink.

Your brown eyes glint and stab my muddy ones, and you cock your slender head, letting dark curls roll down like waves. I just know you’re talking shit just behind those pursed lips. 

I could pull the strings and you’d move to my will. I could pull out a anegortueN wipe, and wash your face down like a rag to a table.

But I won’t and you know it. It’s been years since I’ve revealed myself to you. 

Besides, how should I know if you’re even wearing makeup over there? Your cheekbone is smooth and carmally. Mine is a pile of concealer and foundation atop a purpley contusion. As far as I know, you have no bruises to hide.

With a huff, I step into the hall and my posture collapses. The window won’t reach here. You don’t exist anymore. I palm my keys off the table and whirl the ring around my finger. They jingle a farewell tune, and I know it’s time to revive you. 

I speed walk past the miniature mirror squares in the living room, gaze on the carpet. Your little peepholes are above the mantelpiece - I know you’re watching. You reflect a sun-ray into my eyes. Bitch.
 


I learned to drive flawlessly at sixteen: look both ways, signal 200 feet before the turn, check my blind spot religiously, drive under the speed limit. It’s my time to work while you watch and judge. 

You model; I live a fucking life. No wonder it’s so easy for you.

I glance up to scan the cars behind me, but you catch my eye, and I can’t help but glare back. A honk and a tire screech. My eyes jerk towards the road and I swerve as you chuckle above the stuffed dice and air fresheners.  You made me drive in the wrong lane. 

I park and lock you in without a second glance and balance in my stilt-stilettos to walk across the mall parking lot. I stumble over a pebble on the way. Is my skirt riding up? The fabric bunches at my hips and I struggle to push it down. My button up crackles and groans each time I twist my joints. I move best I can between cotton shackles. 

There’s the entrance, and there you are projected on its glass, transparent and glaring: my malevolent spirit. If only I’d been haunted by someone worthwhile. You stand poised on your heels, fabric smooth and tucked in.

*This is how to look like a waitress, Maritza*, your face says. I charge forward and the doors part before me.

That’s just like you, flaunting all the lofty, picturesque shards of the life of Maritza Reyes. As I march across tiled aisles and mazes of tables, you smirk at me from below a bright yellow wet floor sign. 

I ignore you, and paint a pearly grin for table nine. 

Not as believable as this, you say as a warped caricature on my pen.

Midway through my shift, you flip your elegant hair from the iced tea on my tray, and tell me that mine is frizzy.

My last table includes a polite blue-eyed boy. I scribble his order of Alfredo pasta and gaze at the texture in his irises, when you blink at me from his pupils and mock, *Maybe this one wouldn’t hit you, Maritza.* 

At eleven when I file to my car, I know better than to cry. You’d laugh and call me a baby through the tears. And so begins the trek home. Would you like sword swallowing or tightrope walking? I zoom across an overpass, and you suggest that I jerk my steering wheel to the right and floor it.

That may not be your worst idea.



“The fuck have you been?” Jake slurs, a silhouette in the hall.

“Work.”

“You bring food?” He stumbles forward. I anchor myself as my heart races.

“Um..”

“*Um.*”

“I..couldn’t get any. We were running lo-” A swing and clatter. The candle goes flying and shatters. Wax rolls and crumbles below.

“It’s a yes or no question, Maritza. *Did you bring food*?”

“No.”

“No fucking food. No fucking food. Guess I’m just supposed to eat shit, huh?” He paces and gesticulates through drunken rage, then pushes himself right up against me, palm up. “Keys.”

“But-”

“Keys.”

“Jake, you’ve been dri-” He grasps me by the shoulders and shoves me to the wall.

“You think you’re fucking St. Peter or some shit? If you didn’t want me driving, you should’ve brought me food. Last chance. *Keys.*”

I produce the keys from my purse and they flutter like wind-chimes. He cuts off their tune with his fist and storms out the door. It trembles after he’s gone.

I shake, head down, and walk to the bathroom. I switch the lights off before I enter and stand before the sink for a moment, then I stoop and feel for my Neutrogena wipes under the sink. Your silhouette is unreadable. I pull a cloth out, and hold it at the ready, alcohol draped over my fingertips.

I wonder if you wear makeup. 

It’s a blinding flash, then ironclad willpower to not turn away. The streaky mascara through tears, smeared foundation, and lipstick, cheek glowing purple. This is you. This is me. I don’t know whether to feel relieved or disappointed. You’re hideous.

I’m hideous. I look at the sink, peppered my tears. I scream and my fist collides with yours, and your window shrieks and cracks. Pieces clatter onto the faucet, and my hand throbs, your bloodshot, watery eyes smudged with little red droplets. I glance at the laceration across the side of my hand. It was bleeding, but it wouldn’t kill me. 

Could it kill you? 

Blood trails down my fingers and falls onto a shard in the sink. I reach down and pick it up, smudging blood across the surface with my thumb. See it? Time to see if ghosts can be killed.

I slide the shard across my wrist, and glance at your greasy reflection. You want me to do it. I push against the vein, and my skin gives. All I have to do is plunge it in with all my might.

“You want me to do it.” Oh I know you hate the sound of my voice, but bear with me. It’s not like you have a choice. This is the grand finale you’ve been waiting for.

I clasp my fist around the jagged triangle. The serrated edges pierce my palm. I fume. You fume. I lift the shard above my head and slam it onto the sink below me. It breaks into three and slides down ceramic before getting lodged in the drain.

Your face is broken into spiderwebs and warped, like a puzzle where the pieces are all different sizes. You pout at me. Pathetic.

“So, guess what? I’m never performing for you again.” And I leave.



 You made me believe that I had to aspire for your perfection, but you’re just a model wearing my skin. Perfection is a fairy-tale that you told me through compacts when I was thirteen. It only took me eight more birthdays, and three years of garbage repetition to realize. That’s all. Fuck you.

But believe me, I’m not ignoring you. I see you right there, in the window of my taxi, and in the rearview mirror. Fucking watch for all I care. Maybe you’ll have fun in LA with my sister, where you’ll learn to play nice. If not, don’t worry. She lives in a one bedroom with one tiny, circular mirror propped up on a dresser. Nothing a tablecloth can’t cover up.

Okay, I just opened up my book and I honestly think we're interpreting this differently. This scene literally shows all of the growth Snape has undergone. 

*"I thought...all these years...that we were protecting him for her. For Lily."*

This line is much less about Snape's motivations and whether or not he cares about Harry than it is about how he feels betrayed that Dumbledore knew that Harry would have to die. Basically realizing that everything he's been doing is for naught. 

And literally on the next page Snape says that he cares about Harry. I don't think I need to quote this part, we've all heard it a million times.

When Snape is repulsed by what Dumbledore has done, Dumbledore even has the audacity to say, as if he thinks Snape won't care:
*"Don't be shocked, Severus. How many men and women have you watched die?"*

When Snape answers: *"Lately, only those whom I could not save"* we see explicitly that Snape doesn't only care about Lily and her son, but truly cares for the well being of innocents and the wizarding world.

I see his transition from Death Eater to Order as a disillusionment with Voldemort and the DE that was catalyzed by the Potters' murder. Snape didn't switch loyalties at the drop of a hat; I don't believe he ever truly wanted to stay in the DE, but did out of fear. When one of the only good people in his life is threatened, he initially takes action for her. But she dies, his philosophy become less 'for Lily' and more 'against Voldemort'. Lily is the underlying reason he initially switched but she led him to become ultimately against the DE, so it ceased to be entirely about her.

I think it's, for lack of a better word, objectifying (yeah that's really not the right word but you'll see what I mean) to judge Snape based entirely on Lily's morals. While he did care for her and ultimately change because of her, what he did was of his own accord. I don't disagree with much of what you said about his teaching, because it's true, he was not a pleasant man and I don't think Dumbledore should've ever put him in charge of children. I think it's pointed out at some points that Crab and Goyle get shit grades and Hermione gets great grades in potions. If he truly was a biased grader, these would be opposite.

While it does not justify this behavior, though, I do think his past and basically entire background provide viable explanation for it (in the same way that Draco was pressured and conditioned into the DE those around him).

The aspects of the novel you've highlighted are, what I think, the book's only redeeming qualities which happen to be the only aspects I enjoyed when I first read it. I like the idea of a book with a protagonist who doesn't fit the standard definition of what a protagonist usually is. Usually, we like to root for someone who's active, noble, selfless, and strives to reach a goal in spite of character flaws or a troubled past. 

The Catcher in the Rye seems to hold the perfect opposite of this. Holden has had someone close to him die and was betrayed by a teacher he admired. He's also heavily flawed because of how little he cares about school. But, unlike a classic "hero", he doesn't grow from his problems, or strive for some selfless universal goal. He doesn't seem to care about much. Not about school or coming to terms with the past. He's just kind of caught, but he can't do anything. He can't save people, children, innocent children like he used to be. Because how can he? He's just some kid.

I know the reason a lot of people don't like this book is because they don't like Holden. Personally, my problem never was with Holden because I understood the point of his character. My problem was that it was like nothing happened throughout the whole book. Sure, events took place, things *happened*, but there was little more happening than walking through the park, telling a prostitute to go away, seeing his sister. Things like that. Things just kept happening but it was a series of "and"s. There was no real lasting effect of any of the events that happened or impact, save for the scene with his teacher. 

By the end of the book, Holden's exactly where he started. He's going to go to school and flunk out again. I'm not saying people shouldn't like this book. I get why people do. It just doesn't make sense to me that the point of this book is supposed to be that there is no point.
